narrative: The model estimated your probability of failing the final year at 30%. That does not mean failure is certain—roughly seven in ten similar students would pass—but it is the risk level the school has used to require remedial courses, so treat it as a preventive warning rather than a verdict. The strongest factor behind the flag was your intention about continuing to higher education: you indicated no, while every passing student in the comparison group indicated yes. This was the top-ranked influence and pushed the estimate toward failing. The second-ranked factor was your past class failures. You have none, matching the average for students who passed, so this actually reduced your risk and pushed toward passing. The third-ranked factor was going out with friends. Your low level of going out was also protective: most passing students go out a medium amount, and only about a quarter go out as little as you do, so this modestly pushed toward passing. Even so, the lack of higher-education intention outweighed those protective signals. To improve your position, focus first on setting a clear academic goal and discussing future study or training options with your guardian or school staff. Also consider increasing weekly study time—yours is under two hours, while most passing peers study two to five—and asking for family or school support, especially since you currently receive no family educational support and have no home internet.
